# Problem 1

```{r birthday-function}
birthday_repeated = function(n) {

  birthdays = sample(
    1:365,
    size = n,
    replace = TRUE
  )

  repeated = length(unique(birthdays)) < n

  return(repeated)
}
```

```{r birthday-simulation}
birthday_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(group_size, birthday_repeated)
  )

birthday_prob_df =
  birthday_results_df |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(
    prob_repeat = mean(repeated),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

birthday_prob_df
```

```{r birthday-plot}
birthday_prob_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Shared Birthdays by Group Size",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthdays"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = scales::percent
  )
```

The probability that at least two people share a birthday increases as group size increases. 
The relationship is nonlinear, with the probability increasing rapidly for smaller group sizes 
before gradually approaching 1. The probability exceeds approximately 50% when the group contains 23 people. 
This illustrates the birthday paradox, where shared birthdays become surprisingly likely even in relatively small groups.

# Problem 2

```{r import-data}
file_names =
  tibble(
    file_name = list.files(
      path = "./data",
      pattern = "\\.csv$",
      full.names = TRUE
    )
  )

file_names
```

```{r read-data}
study_df =
  file_names |>
  mutate(
    data = map(file_name, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
  )

study_df
```

```{r tidy-data}
study_tidy_df =
  study_df |>
  mutate(
    arm = case_when(
      str_detect(file_name, "con_") ~ "Control",
      str_detect(file_name, "exp_") ~ "Experimental"
    ),
    subject_id = str_extract(
      basename(file_name), "\\d+"
    )
  ) |>
  select(-file_name) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(str_remove(week, "week_")),
    arm = factor(
      arm,
      levels = c("Control", "Experimental")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

study_tidy_df
```

```{r spaghetti-plot}
study_tidy_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = interaction(arm, subject_id),
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(. ~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly Observations by Treatment Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Treatment Arm"
  )
```

The spaghetti plot shows different longitudinal patterns between the control and experimental groups. 
Observations in the control group remain relatively stable across the eight weeks, 
with some individual variability. In contrast, participants in the experimental group 
generally show increasing observations over time. Although there is variation across individuals, 
the upward trend in the experimental group suggests a positive effect of the experimental intervention 
on the measured outcome. However, since we did not conduct a hypothesis test, 
this descriptive comparison alone does not establish statistical significance.
